latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Enteric infection with Shiga toxin-producing organisms produces watery or bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting, mucosal inflammation, and toxin exposure. The organism, serotype, outbreak link, food exposure, and stool toxin tests are context signals rather than separate disease leaves.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Enteric Shiga toxin release and systemic absorption
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Shiga toxin released in the gut crosses an inflamed intestinal barrier and circulates on blood cells, platelets, microvesicles, or soluble carriers. Antibiotic or antimotility exposure during the diarrheal phase can increase effective toxin exposure in susceptible cases.
Shiga toxin binds Gb3/Gb4-rich target cells, traffics retrograde, inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis, and triggers apoptosis, cytokine release, and prothrombotic endothelial/podocyte signaling.

Renal glomerular endothelial cells, podocytes, and tubular cells become activated or injured, with glycocalyx loss, leukocyte adhesion, VEGF/complement disturbance, capillary swelling, and renal thrombotic microangiopathy.

Shiga toxin-injured glomerular surfaces can amplify alternative complement activation. Complement regulatory variants or anti-factor H biology can increase severity and prolong renal TMA without turning the first-layer diagnosis into complement-mediated TMA.

Activated endothelium, platelets, leukocytes, and vWF-dependent adhesion form platelet-rich thrombi in renal and extrarenal microvessels, consuming platelets and obstructing perfusion. Coagulation tests are usually near-normal compared with DIC.

Erythrocytes fragment while traversing narrowed thrombotic microvessels, producing schistocytes, hemoglobin fall, high LDH, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia with a negative direct Coombs test.

Glomerular and arteriolar TMA, tubular injury, volume depletion, and hypertension produce abrupt creatinine/BUN rise, oliguria or anuria, proteinuria, hematuria, hyperkalemia, acidosis, edema, dialysis need, and later CKD risk.

Severe STEC-HUS can injure CNS, bowel, pancreas, myocardium, and lung through endothelial injury, microthrombosis, hypertension, uremia, and systemic inflammation. CNS involvement is a major mortality driver, especially in adults.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Watery diarrhea is usually the earliest syndrome from enteric STEC infection.
Colonic mucosal injury can progress from watery diarrhea to hemorrhagic colitis.
Cramping abdominal pain tracks colitis severity.
Vomiting and poor intake commonly accompany STEC colitis and worsen dehydration risk.
Fever is present in a minority but signals stronger inflammatory colitis.
Leukocytosis during hemorrhagic colitis correlates with severe toxin-mediated disease and HUS risk.
Inflamed colitis provides the toxin source and mucosal route for systemic exposure.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: strongest for toxin-inducing antibiotics or treatment before HUS is established
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Antibiotic exposure during STEC diarrhea can increase toxin release or HUS risk in susceptible patients.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: strongest when ongoing diarrhea is present
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Slowed transit may prolong toxin exposure and is avoided in suspected STEC diarrhea.
Systemic toxin reaches susceptible Gb3/Gb4-rich targets and initiates cellular injury.
Renal glomerular microvasculature and podocyte-endothelial unit are primary targets of toxin-mediated injury.
Toxin-injured surfaces amplify alternative complement activation and can unmask complement regulatory susceptibility.
Activated injured endothelium and exposed subendothelial structures recruit platelets and leukocytes, forming renal-predominant TMA.
Complement amplification increases endothelial injury and platelet-leukocyte thromboinflammation.
Platelets are consumed in microthrombi; nadirs commonly occur after diarrheal symptoms improve.
Thrombotic microvascular narrowing causes shear fragmentation of erythrocytes.
Intravascular hemolysis and repeated phlebotomy/transfusion course lower hemoglobin.
Fragmented red cells are the peripheral smear signature of MAHA.
Hemolysis and ischemic tissue injury raise LDH, often markedly.
Free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin.
Bone marrow response raises reticulocytes unless limited by marrow disease or nutrient deficiency.
Hemolysis preferentially increases indirect bilirubin.
Renal arteriolar and glomerular thrombi reduce perfusion and filtration.
Direct renal cellular injury combines with microthrombosis to produce AKI.
Creatinine rises with reduced GFR.
BUN rises with renal failure and dehydration.
Reduced renal perfusion and tubular injury can cause oliguria.
Severe renal TMA can progress to anuria and dialysis dependence.
Glomerular injury causes proteinuria.
Glomerular and tubular injury causes microscopic or gross hematuria.
Severe AKI reduces potassium excretion.
AKI, diarrhea, and uremia produce metabolic acidosis.
The renal mechanism is the direct driver of AKI risk.
Anuria, hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or uremia trigger renal replacement therapy need.
Renal ischemia and volume overload can cause severe hypertension.
Salt and water retention produces edema.
CNS endothelial injury, uremia, hypertension, and metabolic derangement cause encephalopathy.
Seizures occur in severe neurologic STEC-HUS.
Neurologic injury is one of the most important extrarenal hazards.
Severe colitis and microvascular injury can produce bowel necrosis, perforation, or late stricture.
Pancreatic microvascular injury can elevate enzymes or cause pancreatitis.
Myocardial microthrombi or demand ischemia can cause troponin elevation and cardiac dysfunction.
STEC-HUS is a platelet-rich TMA; PT/INR is often normal unless shock, liver injury, DIC, or anticoagulants coexist.
aPTT is usually near-normal in isolated STEC-HUS, helping distinguish it from consumptive coagulopathy.
Fibrinogen is usually preserved or elevated as an acute-phase reactant rather than consumed as in decompensated DIC.
Hemolysis is mechanical rather than immune-mediated.
Foodborne, waterborne, daycare, animal, outbreak, or household exposure histories increase prior probability.
Stool toxin/PCR is confirmatory context and should not be required as ordinary presentation ranking evidence.
Culture or serotype identifies organism context but may become negative after diarrhea resolves.
Terminal complement activity is a treatment-context axis for rare severe or complement-amplified cases.
Bone marrow response raises reticulocytes unless limited by marrow disease or nutrient deficiency. Alternate reporting form represented separately from absolute/percent units.
Hemolysis raises indirect bilirubin and can produce icterus/jaundice.
Hemolysis can contribute to AST elevation.
Ischemic organ injury can raise AST.
Hepatic/systemic ischemic injury can raise ALT.
Acute inflammatory or stress physiology can increase neutrophils.

Lifespan outcome hazard for STEC-HUS. Driven by CNS involvement, severe AKI/anuria, dialysis complications, bowel necrosis/perforation, myocardial injury, shock/sepsis overlap, age, and treatment delay.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Bloody diarrhea and compatible food/outbreak context co-occur in STEC colitis.
Vomiting and poor intake amplify prerenal stress on top of renal TMA.
Leukocytosis during colitis is a recognized marker of severe STEC disease and HUS risk.
Very low platelets and procedures increase bleeding hazard, though thrombosis/AKI remain dominant.
Severe anemia increases myocardial oxygen demand mismatch.
LDH rise and hemoglobin fall share MAHA mechanism.
Creatinine and BUN rise together with reduced GFR, with dehydration adding BUN excess.
Oliguria/anuria is a direct clinical trigger for renal replacement therapy when accompanied by uremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, or overload.
Severe hyperkalemia is an acute dialysis trigger.
Severe metabolic acidosis can require dialysis or bicarbonate support.
Severe AKI, metabolic derangements, and fluid overload increase short-term mortality risk.
Need for renal replacement therapy marks severe renal TMA and ICU risk.
Encephalopathy is an observed manifestation of CNS involvement.
Severe CNS involvement is one of the strongest acute mortality drivers.
Bowel necrosis/perforation or severe colitis complications increase mortality through sepsis, surgery, and shock.
Cardiac involvement is rare but dangerous.
Major bleeding can complicate profound thrombocytopenia or invasive support.
Terminal complement blockade can create meningococcal or encapsulated bacterial infection risk that enters outcome through an event hazard.

treatments.drug: Early isotonic volume expansion and renal perfusion support

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Established volume overload limits further fluid and shifts care toward dialysis or diuresis.
Oliguria reduces fluid tolerance despite renal perfusion needs.

side_effects.interpretation: Excess fluid can cause edema or pulmonary edema in oliguric AKI.
Volume loading can worsen hypertension after renal failure is established.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic instability may require CRRT rather than intermittent dialysis.
Vascular access and anticoagulation decisions become more hazardous.

side_effects.interpretation: Access placement and anticoagulation may increase bleeding risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Volume overload and dialysis dependence constrain transfusion speed and amount.

side_effects.interpretation: Transfusion volume can worsen overload in oliguric AKI.

treatments.drug: Platelet transfusion for active bleeding or procedure support

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bleeding or urgent invasive procedure increases the immediate value of platelet support.
Platelet transfusion does not treat the core TMA and can be avoided when there is no bleeding/procedure need.

side_effects.interpretation: Unnecessary platelets may theoretically add substrate to active platelet-rich TMA.

treatments.drug: Stop or avoid antibiotics when STEC is suspected and no invasive bacterial infection requires treatment

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: True invasive bacterial infection may still require antibiotics; STEC-HUS risk is not the only context.
Confirmed Shiga toxin supports withdrawal of unnecessary antibiotic exposure.

side_effects.interpretation: No toxicity axis is applied; the risk is undertreating a separate invasive infection context.

treatments.drug: Stop antimotility agents during suspected STEC diarrhea

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bloody diarrhea increases concern for invasive/toxin-mediated colitis where slowing transit is undesirable.
Hypotension or shock precludes aggressive BP lowering.
Correcting metabolic seizure contributors improves neurologic stabilization.
Uremic encephalopathy requires renal replacement support in addition to antiseizure medication.

side_effects.interpretation: Sedating antiseizure drugs can transiently worsen measured mental status.

treatments.drug: Therapeutic plasma exchange while TTP remains unresolved

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency shifts the active manifold toward TTP where TPE directly changes the mechanism.
Confirmed STEC-HUS has no consistent direct response to TPE except exceptional severe/overlap contexts.
Apheresis line placement and plasma exposure add bleeding and reaction risks.

side_effects.interpretation: Central venous access and procedure-related anticoagulation can add bleeding risk.
Plasma replacement can worsen volume burden.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Evidence and biologic plausibility are strongest when complement amplification is prominent.
Severe neurologic disease is a context where non-supportive rescue therapy is sometimes considered.
C5 blockade increases meningococcal risk and requires vaccination/prophylaxis context.

side_effects.interpretation: Terminal complement blockade increases meningococcal and encapsulated bacterial infection hazard.

age_under_5_years.trajectory_modulation: Higher incidence after STEC exposure; dehydration and renal reserve amplify severity.

older_adult.trajectory_modulation: Lower incidence than children but higher CNS, dialysis, CKD, and mortality risk when disease occurs.

female.trajectory_modulation: Several outbreak and risk-factor studies report higher HUS risk in females after EHEC infection.

undercooked_beef_unpasteurized_or_outbre.trajectory_modulation: Strongly raises prior for STEC enterocolitis before confirmatory stool testing.

no_exposure_identified.trajectory_modulation: Absence of known exposure does not exclude sporadic STEC.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises likelihood of STEC-HUS and indicates stronger mucosal toxin source.

absent_or_nonbloody.trajectory_modulation: Does not exclude STEC-HUS, especially when diarrhea is chronic, resolved, or poorly observed.

present.trajectory_modulation: Volume depletion worsens renal perfusion and increases AKI/dialysis risk.

white_blood_cell_count_high.trajectory_modulation: Leukocytosis is a severity marker for progression from STEC infection to HUS.

risk_factors.factor: Antibiotic exposure during active STEC diarrhea

present.trajectory_modulation: Antibiotic exposure during the toxin-producing diarrheal phase can increase effective toxin exposure and HUS risk; the magnitude depends on drug and timing.

treatment_effect_modulation.treatment: Stop or avoid antibiotics when STEC is suspected and no invasive bacterial infection requires treatment

present.trajectory_modulation: May prolong toxin exposure and worsen colitis/dehydration risk in suspected STEC.

risk_factors.factor: Shiga toxin 2 or high-virulence serotype context

stx2_or_o157_o104_context.trajectory_modulation: Stx2 and high-virulence STEC contexts are associated with higher HUS and CNS/renal severity.

stx1_only_context.trajectory_modulation: Stx1 can cause adult STEC-HUS but average virulence is lower than Stx2 in many cohorts.

present.trajectory_modulation: Complement regulatory variants or anti-factor H biology can amplify and prolong renal TMA after a STEC trigger.

risk_factors.factor: Baseline chronic kidney disease, hypertension, or low renal reserve

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises baseline creatinine and increases dialysis dependence, hypertension, and incomplete renal recovery risk.

supportive_care: Early recognition of diarrheal TMA from serial CBC, creatinine/BUN, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, smear, electrolytes, urinalysis, and blood pressure after STEC-compatible gastroenteritis.
Frequent fluid-balance assessment: strict intake/output, daily weights, urine output, edema, pulmonary exam, and dialysis trigger review.
Renal replacement therapy for severe uremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, or anuria using modality matched to hemodynamic stability.
Packed red blood cell transfusion for clinically significant anemia, myocardial stress, or symptomatic oxygen-delivery deficit.
Avoid platelet transfusion unless active major bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure requires it.
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and antimotility drugs during suspected STEC diarrhea; treat a proven invasive bacterial coinfection as a separate context.
Manage hypertension and volume overload while preserving renal and cerebral perfusion.
Monitor CNS status closely; treat seizures, correct sodium/glucose/uremia/acidosis contributors, and escalate airway/neurocritical support when needed.
Monitor for bowel necrosis/perforation, pancreatitis, myocardial injury, and pulmonary edema when abdominal pain, enzymes, troponin, respiratory status, or hemodynamics worsen.
Send stool Shiga toxin PCR/EIA and culture/serotype early when possible, but do not wait for confirmation to monitor and support a compatible TMA course.
Send ADAMTS13 and coagulation tests to separate TTP/DIC/complement-mediated TMA context; preserve these as confirmatory or differential context rather than deleting presentation evidence.
Long-term nephrology follow-up for CKD, hypertension, proteinuria, hematuria, and dialysis recovery after the acute episode.

For terminal complement blockade consideration, document complement context, meningococcal vaccination/prophylaxis, infection risk, timing, and severity rather than treating it as an automatic therapy.
